explanation: `printf(buffer)` passes the fully-built log line as the *format string* itself, not just data to be printed. Since `buffer` already contains `user_input` verbatim (via `snprintf`), any `%` conversion specifiers embedded in that user-supplied text — like `%s`, `%x`, or `%n` — get interpreted by `printf` as real format directives instead of literal characters. This is the classic format-string vulnerability: it can crash the program (reading a nonexistent vararg), leak stack/memory contents, or with `%n` even write to arbitrary memory. The fix is `printf("%s", buffer)` so the buffer is always treated as plain data.
